author: Claude, from the Whisper transcript, before any report was generated

chapters.title: Welcome: 20 years of open-source Blender, and a health update
Three hard years: hospital, COVID, war, energy and climate
The metaverse hype and who to trust with the next internet
Announcing Blender Lab, and AI as a tool for artists
The freedom to create: three core freedoms
Rethinking Blender Studio, and the problem with pipelines
Add-ons must be GPL; an official extensions platform

key_points: Blender became open source 20 years ago in Amsterdam, and the speaker is healthy again after a serious hospitalization.
The metaverse is being pushed by big corporations that many people no longer trust; Blender, with a large creative community and no shareholders, should step in.
A new initiative, Blender Lab, will gather five to ten top people to work on Blender's future, such as AR/VR, networking and online collaboration.
AI should be a tool that works for artists, under their control, and freely and openly available.
The way to build the metaverse is not to aim for it, but to do nice things for people: tools, sharing, collaboration and a fair living for artists.
The 'freedom to create' slogan rests on three freedoms: open-source software, access to creative resources and production knowledge, and access to markets.
Blender apps let people package blend files with Python-driven UI into their own custom applications, such as viewers or client presentations.
Blender Studio dropped its feature-film plan (the rights went to a production company) and refocuses on small teams sharing production knowledge.
Industrial pipelines serve whoever pays the bills and treat artists as disposable, as the closure of a large Blender-based studio showed.
Hollywood is welcome to contribute to Blender's mission, but Blender will not work for it; Blender serves the much larger rest of the market.
Add-ons are part of Blender and must be GPL; Blender will run an official extensions platform with pre-approved add-ons, alongside commercial marketplaces.
